_comment: 🪝️ Reference registrations for the repo hooks module. Nothing here is linked into production and no external distribution is declared: both oracles are second implementations written inside the case's own 🟦️.ts adapter, and the two decisions that have no oracle at all rest on frozen specification vectors instead. No oracleHostPackages are declared, so nothing enters 🔒️dependencies.json through this manifest.

oracles.rationale: 🛡️ A second implementation of the blocking policy in TypeScript, written from the prose in the case's `🥒️.feature` and the shapes in `🧬️schema/🔣️.json` rather than from the Rust source, and deliberately using a different strategy: the platform's regular expression engine where the subject hand-rolls a character scanner. It is registered as `cross-semio-implementation` because it is NOT independent evidence — it lives in this repository — and the `repo-hooks-blocking-vocabulary` decision beside it records why nothing outside can take its place: which git verbs a monorepo refuses its own agents is a policy this repository invents, and no third-party library adjudicates it. What the second implementation does buy is that a scanning mistake cannot hide, since a regular expression engine and a hand-rolled scanner fail differently.

🗺️ A second implementation of plan extraction and of the fold that keeps a plan's history, written in TypeScript from the stated rules. The lifecycle — ideated on first sight, started on first progress, completed only after starting, abandoned when dropped without ever moving — is this repository's own definition of what an agent's plan means over time; no third-party task or todo library defines it, and the ones that exist define something else. A second implementation is what makes an off-by-one in the fold visible.

📓️ A second implementation of the `[logging]` parse and of the `session.json` record in TypeScript. Both halves are this repository's own: the config file is ours and the record is the shape our own coordinator reads back. The session store is a port in both implementations, so the oracle records into a plain map and the subject into its memory store — neither reaches a disk, a clock or a process, and the comparison is therefore about the record and nothing else.

noOracleDecisions.rationale: The mapping from eight IDEs' native hook events onto one neutral event vocabulary is defined by this repository and by nothing else: the neutral slugs are ours, the tool-kind classification that decides which of them a `PreToolUse` becomes is ours, and each IDE's own documentation stops at the native name. No third-party library consumes any of it, and the IDEs themselves cannot be asked — they emit events, they do not adjudicate mappings, and driving eight editors from a test would put eight GUIs inside a test run. Confidence therefore comes from frozen specification vectors: `🧫️fixtures/🔀️native-events.json` pins the expected neutral event and parent hint beside every native one, written from the hook configurations this repository actually commits (`.claude/settings.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json`, `.windsurf/hooks.json`, `.kiro/agents/repo.json`), so an implementation must agree with the specification rather than with itself; the refusal vectors additionally pin that an unknown native name is an error and never a defaulted event. This decision covers no runtime mutation capability.

Only the outer envelope of the wrapped record is VS Code's; its content rule — allow versus deny, reason versus additional context — and the whole plain-record path with its exit code 2 are this repository's contract with eight editors. Nothing third party produces or consumes either, so there is nothing to compare against. The same is true of the micro-commit delegation argv, which exists so that four git hooks reach one implementation. Confidence comes from frozen specification vectors: every invocation carries the verdict and exit code it must produce, the wrapped/plain distinction is asserted across all eight clients at once, and the delegation is replayed through a recorded process runner that answers exit 127 to any argv it was not given — so a changed argv cannot be mistaken for a delegation that still works. This decision covers no runtime mutation capability: the recorded runner never starts a process.
